objects.name: Observable Universe

reference.notes: Ordinary (baryonic) matter only; with dark matter ~9e53 kg. Width = diameter of the particle horizon (~93 billion ly), computed from the same LambdaCDM model as the Hubble radius - about 3x the Hubble sphere, so it plots on the dashed observable-universe edge.

objects.description: Everything close enough that its light has reached us since the Big Bang - about 93 billion light-years across.

first_appeared.label: today
first_appeared.note: Plotted as it is today; its edge has been growing since the Big Bang (the dashed line).

objects.name: Boötes Void

reference.notes: Diameter ~330 million ly (~100 Mpc). Mass is a rough estimate (underdense matter in that volume).

objects.description: One of the largest known cosmic voids: a nearly empty region ~330 million light-years across in the direction of Boötes.

first_appeared.label: 3 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Voids deepen as matter drains into the cosmic web; big ones emerge over the first few billion years.

objects.name: Laniakea Supercluster

reference.notes: ~1e17 solar masses, ~520 million ly (160 Mpc) across.

objects.description: The galaxy supercluster that contains the Milky Way (printed on the chart as 'LANIKEA').

first_appeared.label: 5 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Superclusters are still assembling; their outlines emerge over billions of years.

objects.name: El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915)

reference.notes: ~2e15 solar masses; width ~2 x r200 (~3.6 Mpc).

objects.description: A massive pair of colliding galaxy clusters about 7 billion light-years away - one of the heaviest distant clusters known.

first_appeared.label: 6.48 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Seen as it was 7.3 billion years ago (redshift 0.87), already assembled.

objects.name: Milky Way

reference.notes: Total mass including dark-matter halo; width = stellar disc (~100,000 ly).

objects.description: Our home galaxy, a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across.

first_appeared.label: 485 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Its oldest stars are ~13 billion years old; the disc built up over the following billions of years.

objects.name: Small Magellanic Cloud

reference.notes: ~7e9 solar masses, ~19,000 ly across.

objects.description: A dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

first_appeared.label: 1.78 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Its oldest stars are roughly 10-12 billion years old.

objects.name: Globular clusters

reference.notes: Typical: 1e5-1e6 solar masses, ~100 ly across.

objects.description: Dense, spherical swarms of hundreds of thousands of old stars orbiting a galaxy.

first_appeared.label: 985 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: The oldest Milky Way globular clusters are about 12.5-13 billion years old.

objects.name: TON 618

reference.notes: ~6.6e10 solar masses.

objects.description: A hyper-luminous quasar powered by one of the most massive black holes known.

first_appeared.label: 2.98 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Seen as it was 10.8 billion years ago (redshift 2.2), already enormous.

objects.name: Cygnus A

reference.notes: Central black hole ~2.5e9 solar masses (the radio galaxy itself is far larger).

objects.description: A powerful radio galaxy whose central supermassive black hole drives jets hundreds of thousands of light-years long.

first_appeared.label: 700 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Billion-solar-mass black holes (quasars) existed within ~700 million years of the Big Bang; Cygnus A's own history is unknown.

objects.name: Sagittarius A*

reference.notes: ~4.3e6 solar masses.

objects.description: The supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022.

first_appeared.label: 1 billion years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Thought to have grown with the young Milky Way; its exact age is unknown.

objects.name: LB-1

reference.notes: The 2019 claim of a ~70 solar-mass black hole; later analyses favour a much smaller black hole or none.

objects.description: A binary system announced in 2019 as hosting a surprisingly heavy stellar black hole; the claim has since been disputed.

first_appeared.label: 200 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Stellar black holes first formed when the earliest massive stars collapsed, ~200 million years after the Big Bang.

objects.name: V616 Monocerotis (A0620-00)

reference.notes: Identification inferred from the label 'MONOCEROTIS'; ~6.6 solar masses.

objects.description: Probably V616 Monocerotis, one of the nearest known stellar-mass black holes (~3,000 light-years away).

first_appeared.label: 200 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Stellar black holes first formed when the earliest massive stars collapsed, ~200 million years after the Big Bang.

objects.name: Primordial black hole

reference.notes: Hypothetical. Mass chosen near where the poster draws it; a black hole's width follows from its mass (Schwarzschild diameter), so it sits exactly on the black-hole line. The poster draws it slightly inside the forbidden region.

objects.description: Unlabelled icon on the Schwarzschild line inside the 'primordial black holes*' band: a hypothetical black hole formed in the early universe.

first_appeared.label: 10^-22 seconds after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: If primordial black holes exist, one forms when its mass fits inside the horizon: t ~ GM/c^3.

objects.name: Neutron star
objects.description: Unlabelled small dark sphere (tentative): a collapsed stellar core ~20 km across, denser than an atomic nucleus.

first_appeared.label: 200 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: The first supernovae, ~200 million years after the Big Bang, left the first neutron stars.

objects.name: White dwarfs
objects.description: Unlabelled white spheres (tentative): Earth-sized remnants of Sun-like stars, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

first_appeared.label: 300 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Stars of a few solar masses live tens to hundreds of millions of years before leaving white dwarfs.

objects.name: Sun
objects.description: Our star: a G-type main-sequence star holding 99.8% of the Solar System's mass.

first_appeared.label: 4.6 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Formed 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.

objects.name: Red dwarfs

reference.notes: Values for Proxima Centauri.

objects.description: Unlabelled red spheres (tentative): small cool stars, the most common kind in the galaxy. The 'STARS & PLANETS' arrow points here.

first_appeared.label: 785 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Small, long-lived stars; the oldest known are ~13 billion years old.

objects.name: Brown dwarf
objects.description: Unlabelled banded sphere (tentative): a 'failed star' of ~13-80 Jupiter masses, too light to fuse hydrogen.

first_appeared.label: 785 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Formed like stars, from the earliest generations of star formation.

objects.name: Jupiter
objects.description: The largest planet, more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

first_appeared.label: 4.6 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: The first planet to form, within a few million years of the Sun.

objects.name: Saturn
objects.description: Unlabelled ringed planet: the gas giant whose average density is lower than water's.

objects.name: Uranus
objects.description: Unlabelled cyan planet: the ice giant that rotates on its side.

objects.name: Neptune
objects.description: Unlabelled blue planet: the outermost ice giant.

objects.name: Earth
objects.description: Our home planet - the densest planet in the Solar System.

objects.name: Venus
objects.description: Unlabelled tan planet with an arrow pointing at Earth (tentative: Venus, Earth's near-twin in size).

objects.name: Mercury
objects.description: Unlabelled grey planet (tentative): the smallest planet.

objects.name: Mars
objects.description: Unlabelled orange planet (tentative): about half Earth's diameter.

objects.name: Moon
objects.description: Earth's natural satellite, about a quarter of Earth's diameter.

first_appeared.label: 4.51 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Probably formed from the debris of a giant impact on the young Earth.

objects.name: Pluto
objects.description: Unlabelled pale body with an arrow pointing at the Moon (tentative: Pluto).

objects.name: Ceres
objects.description: Unlabelled small grey body (tentative): the largest object in the asteroid belt.

objects.name: Enceladus
objects.description: A small icy moon of Saturn that sprays water from a subsurface ocean.

first_appeared.label: 4.5 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Some studies suggest Saturn's inner moons could be as young as ~100 million years.

objects.name: Phobos

reference.notes: Mean diameter.

objects.description: The larger of Mars's two small, lumpy moons.

first_appeared.label: 4.3 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Origin debated: captured asteroid or debris from an impact on Mars.

objects.name: Deimos

reference.notes: Mean diameter.

objects.description: The smaller, outer moon of Mars.

first_appeared.label: 4.3 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Origin debated: captured asteroid or debris from an impact on Mars.

objects.name: 25143 Itokawa

reference.notes: Mean diameter; 535 x 294 x 209 m.

objects.description: A peanut-shaped rubble-pile asteroid sampled by Japan's Hayabusa probe in 2005.

first_appeared.label: 1.5 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: A rubble pile that reassembled after its parent asteroid was shattered; estimates vary widely.

objects.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
objects.description: The largest of the Giza pyramids, built around 2560 BCE.

first_appeared.label: 4.59 thousand years ago
first_appeared.note: Built around 2560 BCE.

objects.name: Sphere (Las Vegas)

reference.notes: Width (516 ft) is reliable; mass is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

objects.description: A spherical entertainment venue opened in 2023, wrapped in LED panels - 157 m wide and 112 m tall.

first_appeared.label: 3 years ago
first_appeared.note: Opened in September 2023.

objects.name: Tree

reference.notes: Values for General Sherman (height 84 m); the chart position (~1e6 kg, ~11 m) fits a giant sequoia.

objects.description: Unlabelled tree icon between the Sphere and the whale; its position (~1e6 kg, ~11 m) matches a giant sequoia, the most massive tree species.

first_appeared.label: 385 million years ago
first_appeared.note: The first trees grew about 385 million years ago; General Sherman itself is ~2,200 years old.

objects.name: Blue whale
objects.description: The largest animal known to have ever lived, up to ~30 m long.

first_appeared.label: 4.5 million years ago
first_appeared.note: Baleen whales became giants within roughly the last 4.5 million years.

objects.name: Hippopotamus
objects.description: Unlabelled hippopotamus beside the blue whale.

first_appeared.label: 2.5 million years ago
first_appeared.note: The modern hippo genus goes back a few million years.

objects.name: Humans
objects.description: Homo sapiens - a typical adult is about 1.7 m tall and 70 kg.

first_appeared.label: 300 thousand years ago
first_appeared.note: Homo sapiens appeared about 300,000 years ago.

objects.name: Soccer ball
objects.description: Unlabelled football (soccer ball); a regulation size-5 ball is ~22 cm across and ~430 g.

first_appeared.label: 163 years ago
first_appeared.note: Association football's rules were standardised in 1863.

objects.name: Hedgehog
objects.description: A small spiny mammal, typically 15-30 cm long.

first_appeared.label: 15 million years ago
first_appeared.note: Hedgehogs have looked much the same for ~15 million years.

objects.name: US penny
objects.description: A US one-cent coin: 19.05 mm across, 2.5 g.

first_appeared.label: 233 years ago
first_appeared.note: The first US cent was struck in 1793; today's zinc version dates from 1982.

objects.name: Ladybug
objects.description: A small beetle (family Coccinellidae), typically 5-8 mm long.

first_appeared.label: 140 million years ago
first_appeared.note: Ladybird beetles are thought to date from the Cretaceous; their exact origin is uncertain.

objects.name: Grain of salt
objects.description: A single crystal of table salt, about 0.3 mm on a side. It sits on the 1 Planck-mass line.

first_appeared.label: 3.5 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Salt crystals form when seawater evaporates; Earth's oldest evaporite deposits are ~3.5 billion years old.

objects.name: Red blood cell
objects.description: A disc-shaped cell ~7.5 µm across that carries oxygen around the body.

first_appeared.label: 500 million years ago
first_appeared.note: Haemoglobin-filled red cells evolved in early vertebrates, roughly 500 million years ago.

objects.name: Bacterium

reference.notes: E. coli.

objects.description: A single-celled microbe; E. coli is about 2 µm long and weighs about a picogram.

first_appeared.label: 3.8 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Life on Earth is at least ~3.5-3.8 billion years old.

objects.name: Virus

reference.notes: SARS-CoV-2 (the icon is a coronavirus).

objects.description: A virus particle - SARS-CoV-2, for example, is about 100 nm across and weighs about a femtogram.

first_appeared.label: 3.5 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: Viruses leave no fossils; they are probably nearly as old as cellular life.

objects.name: RNA strand

reference.notes: Representative ~1,000-nucleotide RNA (~330 kDa); real RNAs span orders of magnitude.

objects.description: A strand of ribonucleic acid; its size depends entirely on its length, so values are representative.

first_appeared.label: 4 billion years ago
first_appeared.note: RNA may predate DNA and proteins (the 'RNA world'), ~4 billion years ago.

objects.name: Oxygen atom
objects.description: Element 8, the third most abundant element in the universe.

first_appeared.label: 200 million years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Oxygen is forged in stars; the first supernovae spread it ~200 million years after the Big Bang.

objects.name: Helium atom
objects.description: Element 2, mostly forged in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

first_appeared.label: 100 thousand years after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Helium nuclei formed in the first minutes; neutral helium atoms ~100,000 years later, before hydrogen atoms.

objects.name: Fundamental particles

reference.notes: Electron used as the representative particle.

objects.description: Quarks, leptons and bosons - this corner of the triangle is expanded in the 'Fundamental Particles' inset.

first_appeared.label: 10^-12 seconds after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Quarks, leptons and the W and Z gained their masses when the Higgs field switched on, ~10^-12 s after the Big Bang.

objects.name: X and Y bosons

reference.notes: Grand-unified-theory scale, ~1e15 GeV/c^2. Never observed.

objects.description: Hypothetical bosons of grand unified theories, near 10^24 eV on the energy axis; never observed.

first_appeared.label: 10^-36 seconds after the Big Bang
first_appeared.note: Hypothetical: would belong to the grand-unification era, before ~10^-36 s.

objects.name: Dark exoplanets
objects.description: Marked hypothetical on the chart and drawn as a question-mark icon; no position is physically implied.
